west central Ohio.

outdoor plants may be killed if left uncovered.

More than 1,000 public housing units in Hamilton, Middletown to be modernized

In 2022, Butler County commissioned a HUD-required housing study that identified affordable housing as the biggest housing issue in the county.

  • Denise G. Callahan - Contributing Writer

    Denise Callahan

  • Oct 18, 2026
  • 15 hrs ago
  • Facebook

The Butler Metropolitan Housing Authority has embarked on renovating 94% of its public housing stock in Hamilton and Middletown — and there’s a chance they could up the county’s affordable housing inventory.

The housing authority, now known as OneCanopi, is in the process of spending roughly $146.5 million “modernizing” 1,030 of its 1,096 housing units or nearly 94% of its housing portfolio. It is upgrading 492 of 510 units in Hamilton, spending around $71.5 million, averaging roughly $145,000 per unit.

In Middletown it is upgrading 538 of 586 units, spending roughly $75 million on construction and $140,000 per unit.

“Housing is essential infrastructure. When families have stable housing, they are better positioned to work, pursue education, raise their children, and move toward greater independence,” OneCanopi President and CEO Timothy Butler said. “That is why this investment matters. It allows us to modernize aging homes, strengthen neighborhoods and better serve the families who live here.”

Butler told the Journal-News they have just started Phase 3 of the renovation project and plan to wrap it all up by 2028. Efforts are supported by a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development program known as Rental Assistance Demonstration. It allows for partnering with investors to raise funds for the upgrades.

The upgrades to the apartment buildings include new kitchens, bathrooms, plumbing, accessibility improvements and addressing other infrastructure that has “faced years of aging conditions and underinvestment.” Tax credits are the incentive for investors.

“In that joint structure, that development partner goes after private equity that’s interested in the tax credits that is associated with the deal,” Butler said. “Once those equity partners invest the funds and the projects are filled with qualified residents who needed affordable housing they can then take advantage of those tax credits over a period of years.”

Butler said there are 66 remaining units that still need attention, but they are mainly single-family and “scatter-site” units which aren’t as attractive to investors. HUD recently announced updates to its demolition and disposition program and that may address the needs for those units, he said.

Those decisions haven’t been made yet.

New direction for HUD

“Public housing should not be synonymous with blighted or derelict buildings,” said HUD Secretary Scott Turner said about the program updates. “HUD is enhancing local housing authorities’ ability to rehabilitate failing projects and breathe new life into their communities.”

Butler said the company’s new concept isn’t just about providing housing — they have positioned themselves to align with the new direction HUD is going at the behest of the Trump administration.

“We just set up a non-profit subsidiary for resident services to offer people the job readiness support, the mental health counseling they need, educational support they need, financial literacy, all the things they need,” Butler said. “And we just started a Section 13 program with some of our new funding that offers real housing authority jobs to our residents to help them be more self-sufficient.”

This new investment-based approach to public housing may also allow the agency to introduce much-needed new affordable housing units into Butler County’s housing stock, “What all of that does, all of it, positions me to go do more development deals, expand our footprint and that creates new units,” Butler said.

In 2022, the county commissioned a HUD-required housing study that identified affordable housing as the biggest housing issue in the county. There are more than 6,300 renters and around 2,700 homeowners earning less than the median income in the county and are paying half their income on housing.

Mindy Muller, president and CEO of Community Development Professionals, who administers the federal permanent supportive housing program for the county, said OneCanopi’s efforts are appreciated.

“Meeting the diverse housing needs of our community requires a range of housing options at varying income levels. Housing authorities are critical partners in a community’s housing ecosystem, and I am grateful for OneCanopi’s efforts to modernize its current properties,” Muller said. “HUD has offered opportunity for housing authorities to add units to their housing stock, and I would support any effort by OneCanopi to take advantage of this federal investment to increase affordable housing in Butler County.”
